title: Earth and Space Sciences
description: Connect cosmic history, Earth systems, geology, weather, climate, and sustainable decisions.

lessons.title: Scale, measurement and models
lessons.reading: Earth scientists combine observations at different spatial and temporal scales. A model is a purposeful simplification with assumptions and limits. Compare claims with data and account for measurement uncertainty. Patterns can reveal a process without making every correlation causal.
lessons.worked: A rock sample, satellite image, and global climate record represent different scales of evidence.

application.prompt: Which is strongest support for a scientific claim?
application.explanation: Evidence must address the claim and be open to checking or replication.

vocab.definition: A simplified representation used to explain or predict.
The spatial or temporal extent of an observation.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Evidence must address the claim and be open to checking or replication.

lessons.title: Coordinates, contours and gradients
lessons.reading: Latitude measures north-south position and longitude east-west position. Contour lines connect equal elevations. Closely spaced contours indicate steeper slopes; a gradient is change in a field quantity divided by distance. Read map intervals and units before calculating.
lessons.worked: A rise of 100 meters over 2 kilometers has gradient 50 meters per kilometer.

application.prompt: Closer contour lines generally indicate…
application.explanation: The same elevation change occurs over a shorter horizontal distance.

vocab.definition: A line joining locations with equal elevation.
Change in a field value divided by distance.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: The same elevation change occurs over a shorter horizontal distance.

lessons.title: Cosmic evidence and stars
lessons.reading: Light carries information about composition, motion, and temperature. Stellar spectra reveal elements and Doppler shifts. Galaxy redshifts support expansion of the universe. Stars form when gravity gathers material; fusion changes nuclei and releases energy.
lessons.worked: Spectral lines shifted toward longer wavelengths indicate recession in a Doppler interpretation.

application.prompt: A star's emission spectrum most directly helps identify…
application.explanation: Atoms and ions produce characteristic spectral features.

vocab.definition: Radiation separated by wavelength or frequency.
A shift of spectral features toward longer wavelengths.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Atoms and ions produce characteristic spectral features.

lessons.title: Stellar lifecycles and elements
lessons.reading: A star's mass strongly affects its lifetime and eventual fate. Nuclear fusion builds heavier nuclei up to limits set by stellar processes; some heavier elements require other energetic events. The Sun's energy originates from hydrogen fusion, not ordinary burning.
lessons.worked: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium while releasing energy.

application.prompt: The Sun's main energy source is…
application.explanation: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy in the Sun's core.

vocab.definition: Combining light nuclei into heavier nuclei.
Changes in stars over their lifetimes.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy in the Sun's core.

lessons.title: Gravity and planetary motion
lessons.reading: Gravity acts between masses and supports orbital motion. An orbit is continuous motion under gravity rather than a state with no gravity. Planetary orbits are approximately ellipses. Orbital speed varies with position; objects nearer a central body move faster along a given elliptical orbit.
lessons.worked: Earth moves faster near perihelion than near aphelion.

application.prompt: At the closest point of an elliptical orbit, an object generally moves…
application.explanation: Gravitational orbital dynamics connect smaller orbital distance with greater speed along that orbit.

vocab.definition: A path followed under gravitational interaction.
A closed curve with two focal points.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Gravitational orbital dynamics connect smaller orbital distance with greater speed along that orbit.

lessons.title: Earth, Moon and Sun cycles
lessons.reading: Earth's rotation produces daily apparent sky motion. Its tilted axis and revolution produce seasons, not changing distance from the Sun. Moon phases depend on viewing illuminated portions; eclipses require alignment and do not occur at every new or full Moon.
lessons.worked: Northern Hemisphere summer occurs when that hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

application.prompt: What primarily causes Earth's seasons?
options: Changes in the Sun's daily size
application.explanation: Tilt changes sunlight angle and day length through the year.

vocab.definition: The angle between a rotation axis and the perpendicular to an orbital plane.
The visible fraction and arrangement of the Moon's illuminated face.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Tilt changes sunlight angle and day length through the year.

lessons.title: Tides and gravitational differences
lessons.reading: Tides arise from differences in gravitational influence across Earth, especially from the Moon and also the Sun. Earth's rotation carries locations through changing tidal patterns. Alignment of Sun, Earth, and Moon affects tidal range; local coastline and seafloor shape actual timing and height.
lessons.worked: New and full Moon alignments generally produce greater tidal ranges than quarter Moon configurations.

application.prompt: Spring tides are associated with…
application.explanation: Aligned solar and lunar tidal effects generally increase the range between high and low water.

vocab.definition: The difference between high and low water levels.
A relatively large tidal range associated with solar-lunar alignment.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Aligned solar and lunar tidal effects generally increase the range between high and low water.

lessons.title: Minerals and the rock cycle
lessons.reading: Minerals have characteristic compositions and structures. Igneous rocks form from solidified melt, sedimentary rocks from accumulated material or precipitation, and metamorphic rocks through solid-state changes. Weathering, erosion, heat, pressure, melting, and crystallization connect these categories.
lessons.worked: A rock recrystallized by heat and pressure without melting is metamorphic.

application.prompt: Which process produces an igneous rock?
application.explanation: Cooling and crystallization of magma or lava produce igneous rocks.

vocab.definition: A naturally occurring inorganic solid with a characteristic structure and composition.
Solid-state alteration by heat, pressure, or fluids.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Cooling and crystallization of magma or lava produce igneous rocks.

lessons.title: Relative and numerical dating
lessons.reading: Superposition orders undeformed sedimentary layers from older below to younger above. Cross-cutting structures are younger than the rocks they cut. Radioactive decay supplies numerical ages under appropriate assumptions. Fossils and unconformities help correlate incomplete records.
lessons.worked: A fault cutting three rock layers formed after those layers were deposited.

application.prompt: A dike cuts layers A and B. Which is necessarily true?
options: The dike is younger than both layers
The dike is older than both
application.explanation: A cross-cutting feature must postdate the material it cuts.

vocab.definition: A surface representing missing geologic time.
The time required for half of a radioactive isotope population to decay.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: A cross-cutting feature must postdate the material it cuts.

lessons.title: Plate boundaries and evidence
lessons.reading: Lithospheric plates move over the underlying mantle. Interior heat supports mantle convection; seismic-wave patterns help infer layered internal structure. The mantle is mostly solid but can flow over geologic time. Divergent boundaries form new crust; convergent boundaries can subduct or build mountains; transform boundaries accommodate sideways motion. Earthquake patterns, magnetic stripes, and rock ages support plate tectonics.
lessons.worked: Ocean-floor rocks generally become older farther from a mid-ocean ridge.

application.prompt: New oceanic crust commonly forms at…
application.explanation: Mantle-derived melt rises and solidifies as plates move apart at ridges.

vocab.definition: One plate descending beneath another.
The theory of moving lithospheric plates and their interactions.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Mantle-derived melt rises and solidifies as plates move apart at ridges.

lessons.title: Earthquakes, volcanoes and risk
lessons.reading: Earthquakes release energy through seismic waves. Wave arrival patterns help locate events; hazard differs from risk because exposure and vulnerability matter. Volcano behavior depends on magma and setting. Design solutions reduce impacts but cannot eliminate all uncertainty.
lessons.worked: Building codes and evacuation plans can reduce losses without preventing tectonic activity.

application.prompt: Which action reduces earthquake risk rather than stopping earthquakes?
application.explanation: Retrofitting reduces vulnerability, one component of risk.

vocab.definition: Energy traveling through or along Earth after a disturbance.
Potential harm considering hazard, exposure, and vulnerability.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Retrofitting reduces vulnerability, one component of risk.

lessons.title: Weathering, erosion and deposition
lessons.reading: Weathering breaks or alters material in place; erosion transports it; deposition leaves it behind. Water, wind, ice, and gravity act differently across particle sizes and landscapes. Transport capacity depends on the moving medium's energy, not just particle availability.
lessons.worked: As a stream slows, it can deposit larger particles it no longer carries.

application.prompt: Which process is transport of sediment by a river?
application.explanation: Erosion includes removal and movement; deposition is settling after transport.

vocab.definition: Removal and transport of Earth material.
Accumulation of transported sediment.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Erosion includes removal and movement; deposition is settling after transport.

lessons.title: The water cycle and reservoirs
lessons.reading: Water moves among atmosphere, surface, groundwater, ice, and organisms. Solar energy drives evaporation and gravity drives downward flow. Permeability and porosity influence infiltration and groundwater storage. Human withdrawal can exceed replenishment.
lessons.worked: Paving a permeable area often increases runoff and reduces infiltration.

application.prompt: Replacing soil with impermeable pavement usually increases…
application.explanation: Impermeable surfaces prevent some water from entering the ground.

vocab.definition: Entry of water into the ground.
A permeable geologic unit capable of storing and transmitting groundwater.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Impermeable surfaces prevent some water from entering the ground.

lessons.title: Energy, pressure and winds
lessons.reading: Unequal solar heating drives atmospheric circulation. Warm air can expand and rise, and pressure differences help drive winds. Earth's rotation deflects large-scale motion through the Coriolis effect. Land and water heat differently, producing local circulation patterns.
lessons.worked: During a typical sunny day, a sea breeze can move from cooler water toward warmer land.

application.prompt: Winds are primarily driven by…
application.explanation: Pressure gradients exert forces on air; rotation and surface effects alter the resulting flow.

vocab.definition: Force exerted by air per unit area.
Apparent deflection associated with observing motion on a rotating Earth.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Pressure gradients exert forces on air; rotation and surface effects alter the resulting flow.

lessons.title: Moisture, fronts and forecasting
lessons.reading: Relative humidity compares actual water vapor with the amount associated with saturation at that temperature. Cooling air can cause condensation. Fronts separate air masses; their movement helps explain changing weather. Forecasts combine observations with models and express uncertainty.
lessons.worked: Air cooled to its dew point can begin condensing water vapor into droplets.

application.prompt: Cloud droplets commonly form when air…
options: Has no particles in any circumstances
application.explanation: Cooling reduces the saturation vapor pressure and can make condensation favorable.

vocab.definition: The temperature at which air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure and vapor content.
A boundary between air masses.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Cooling reduces the saturation vapor pressure and can make condensation favorable.

lessons.title: Oceans redistribute energy
lessons.reading: Surface currents respond to winds, rotation, and continents. Density differences related to temperature and salinity contribute to deeper circulation. Ocean circulation redistributes energy and influences regional climate. A warming or freshening region can change density and alter patterns without stopping every current.
lessons.worked: Warm water transported poleward can moderate nearby climates.

application.prompt: Ocean circulation affects climate partly by…
application.explanation: Transport moves energy between regions, while local conditions and feedbacks still differ.

vocab.definition: Large-scale movement of ocean water.
Density-related circulation influenced by temperature and salinity.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Transport moves energy between regions, while local conditions and feedbacks still differ.

lessons.title: Climate patterns and evidence
lessons.reading: Climate describes distributions of weather over longer periods. Latitude, altitude, oceans, topography, and circulation influence regional patterns. Ice cores, sediments, and other proxies extend records beyond instruments. A short cold event does not disprove a long-term warming trend.
lessons.worked: A coastal region may have smaller annual temperature swings than a similar inland region.

application.prompt: Which describes climate rather than a single weather event?
application.explanation: Climate concerns long-term statistical patterns rather than one event.

vocab.definition: Long-term patterns and statistics of weather.
An indirect record used to infer past conditions.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Climate concerns long-term statistical patterns rather than one event.

lessons.title: Carbon, energy and feedback
lessons.reading: Greenhouse gases absorb and emit infrared radiation, affecting Earth's energy balance. Carbon cycles among air, ocean, life, and rocks. Feedback can amplify or oppose a change. Reduced ice reflectivity can amplify warming by increasing absorbed solar energy.
lessons.worked: Melting reflective ice can expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight.

application.prompt: Ice melt exposing dark ocean is usually a…
application.explanation: Darker surfaces absorb more energy, reinforcing the initial warming.

vocab.definition: The fraction of incoming radiation reflected by a surface.
A response that amplifies or opposes an initial change.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Darker surfaces absorb more energy, reinforcing the initial warming.

lessons.title: Resources and human impacts
lessons.reading: Resources are unevenly distributed by geologic processes. Extraction and use have environmental and social effects. Renewable does not mean impact-free or unlimited. Evaluate evidence for benefits, costs, access, and long-term effects before comparing resource strategies.
lessons.worked: Groundwater can be depleted even though the water cycle continually operates.

application.prompt: A renewable resource can be depleted locally when…
application.explanation: Renewability describes replenishment processes, not a guarantee of unlimited supply at any location.

vocab.definition: A resource replenished on human-relevant timescales under suitable conditions.
Meeting needs while maintaining future environmental and resource capacity.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Renewability describes replenishment processes, not a guarantee of unlimited supply at any location.

lessons.title: Evaluate solutions across systems
lessons.reading: An Earth-system solution may shift effects among atmosphere, water, land, and communities. Define criteria and constraints, test alternatives, and compare trade-offs with data. Hazard reduction and climate mitigation are different goals and can require complementary designs.
lessons.worked: A flood barrier may protect one neighborhood while altering water flow elsewhere.

application.prompt: Which comparison best evaluates a proposed flood design?
options: A guarantee of zero future rain
Risk reduction, cost, habitat effects, and downstream impacts
application.explanation: Multiple criteria reveal trade-offs and effects beyond the immediate site.

vocab.definition: Action reducing a hazard's impact or the drivers of a problem.
A choice gaining one benefit while giving up another.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Multiple criteria reveal trade-offs and effects beyond the immediate site.
